analysis.one_liner: Bans pharmacy benefit managers from keeping secret drug-pricing spreads and clawing back pharmacy payments.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee approved the bill in December 2023, but the full Senate never voted, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers are middlemen that health plans hire to manage prescription drug coverage. This bill would make it illegal for them to charge a health plan more for a drug than they pay the pharmacy and pocket the difference. It would stop them from arbitrarily clawing back money they already paid pharmacies or raising pharmacy fees to offset federal reimbursement changes. PBMs could keep operating largely as they do, but only if they pass all rebates and discounts to health plans and fully disclose their costs, fees, and markups, and the bill adds FTC and state-enforcement powers, annual disclosure reports, a government study of the PBM market, and whistleblower protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with pharmacy insurance, who would benefit from lower drug costs and premiums as PBMs lose the ability to quietly keep the spread between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive. Independent and community pharmacies, many of them small businesses, would stop having reimbursements clawed back after payment. Employers and government programs that buy drug coverage would see the full economics of what they are paying for, backed by FTC enforcement, state attorney general lawsuits, and whistleblower protections for insiders who report violations.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal for a PBM to charge a health plan a different amount for a drug's cost or dispensing fee than it reimburses the pharmacy, where the PBM keeps the difference.
Prohibits PBMs from arbitrarily, unfairly, or deceptively clawing back reimbursement payments to pharmacies, with narrow exceptions for fraudulent claims or services not rendered.
Prohibits PBMs from raising pharmacy fees or lowering reimbursements to offset reimbursement changes directed by the federal government in federally funded health plans.
Lets a PBM avoid the pricing prohibitions only by passing 100 percent of rebates and discounts to the health plan and fully disclosing prices, fees, markups, and manufacturer remuneration.
Requires PBMs to report annually to the FTC and HHS on plan-versus-pharmacy payment differences, pharmacy fees, clawbacks, formulary tier changes, and self-preferencing toward affiliated pharmacies.

Authorizes the FTC to enforce the bill as an unfair or deceptive practice with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation (each day counting separately), and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf.

Protects whistleblowers at PBMs, health plans, drug makers, and pharmacies from retaliation, with jury trial access, double back pay, and no enforcement of arbitration agreements covering those claims.
Directs the GAO to study PBM market share among the ten largest firms, rebate and fee practices, formulary steering toward high-rebate drugs, and whether plans pay PBMs more than PBMs pay pharmacies.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers — the large firms that negotiate drug prices for insurers — would bear the cost, losing the pricing spreads and clawbacks this bill targets and paying penalties if they violate it. Some of that cost pressure could show up in PBM fees or pharmacy reimbursement structures; the bill's exception lets PBMs keep their role entirely if they pass through all rebates and disclose their finances, so the cost lands mostly on the PBM business model rather than on patients directly.

drawbacks.text: PBMs can escape the core prohibitions entirely by passing along 100 percent of price concessions and disclosing their costs, which leaves the industry's business model in place rather than restructuring the drug supply chain.

The clawback ban is qualified: it reaches only clawbacks that are arbitrary, unfair, or deceptive, and allows an affirmative defense that the conduct was reasonably necessary for legal compliance, patient safety, or patient access, giving PBM lawyers room to argue most practices are legitimate.

Companies could attempt to pass compliance costs through to pharmacies or health plans, and full contract disclosure could reduce the negotiating leverage PBMs currently use to extract discounts from drug makers.
The bill creates new FTC reporting and enforcement duties, and costs of the reporting regime fall on PBM firms and their smaller contracting partners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed at a middleman layer whose pricing spreads and clawbacks raise costs for patients, employers, government programs, and pharmacies. The bill is deliberately soft on the industry's structure: a PBM can comply just by passing rebates through and disclosing everything, so the strongest version of the objection is that this is a transparency-and-enforcement bill rather than a redesign of drug pricing. The main honest cost is that PBM compliance could shift some pricing dynamics between PBMs, pharmacies, and plans, though the bill protects state laws and leaves existing PBM authority intact. On balance, the trade favors patients and independent pharmacies over the PBM firms that profit from the current opacity.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill in March 2023 and formally reported it with an amendment in December 2023, placing it on the Senate calendar, but it never came to the floor and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 26, 2023, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On March 22, 2023, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On December 13, 2023, the committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without a written report.
On December 13, 2023, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 283.
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025, having never received a vote on the Senate floor and never being taken up by the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large PBM firms benefit because the bill never became law, leaving their current pricing spreads, fees, and clawback practices unregulated at the federal level. Patients and pharmacies remain in the pre-bill status quo without new transparency or enforcement protections.

against.role: Industry (including the largest national PBM firms and their trade groups)
against.what_they_did: The bill targets PBM pricing spreads, clawbacks, and fee practices that are central to the industry's revenue model; no record source shows the industry's lobbying here, but the bill died before any floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and its cosponsors split 10 Republican to 4 Democrat, a strongly bipartisan roster, though no roll-call vote was ever taken on the bill.

industries.note: The bill targets the PBM revenue model directly: it bans keeping the spread between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive, bans arbitrary clawbacks, requires 100 percent rebate pass-through and full disclosure, and adds FTC penalties and state enforcement. A PBM can avoid the core prohibitions only by passing all rebates to plans and disclosing its finances, so the industry's role survives only under far greater transparency.

Community pharmacies would stop having reimbursements clawed back after payment and would be protected from fee increases used to offset federal reimbursement changes. Many operate on thin margins, so this targets their survival directly.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers offering drug coverage
industries.note: Plans and payers gain transparency into PBM costs, rebates, and markups, and gain from the ban on PBM spread pricing. But PBM services remain the channel through which pharmacy benefits are managed, so the bill does not remove the middleman, it just constrains and discloses it.

The bill requires disclosure of the full remuneration PBMs receive from manufacturers, including rebates and fees, which could expose and pressure rebate arrangements that steer patients toward higher-rebate drugs. Manufacturers are not otherwise regulated by this bill.
